title: Pentheus
source: P. Ovidius Naso, Metamorphoses, ed. Hugo Magnus (Gotha: F.A. Perthes), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-latinLit phi0959.phi006.perseus-lat2, sha256 fb3fdb1d8a4a3b82. Collated against The Latin Library (cltk mirror) as a disagreement detector only. Original spelling kept. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed Classical (restored) Latin, applied consistently. All translations were made fresh from the Latin for Lectorium.
about: Pentheus, king of Thebes, has refused to admit the new god Bacchus, and his men bring him a captive worshipper instead of the god himself. Almost all of this part is that prisoner's answer: Acoetes, a Maeonian fisherman turned helmsman, tells how his crew took a sleeping boy aboard as plunder, swore to carry him to Naxos, and steered the other way — and what the boy turned out to be. Pentheus hears the story out, orders him tortured to death, and then climbs Cithaeron himself to see the rites, where his mother and her sisters are dancing. The Latin is dactylic hexameter and the sentences run freely across the verse lines, so the unit you tap often spans several; the line numbers are the standard way to cite the poem.
advisory: This part ends with Pentheus torn apart alive by his mother and her sisters, and the poem names the damage — the right hand wrenched off as he begs, the other arm torn away, the maimed stumps held up for his mother to see, the severed head clutched in her bloody fingers; Lectorium presents the text as written.

sentences.t:
Adspicit hunc Pentheus oculis, quos ira tremendos
fecerat, et quamquam poenae vix tempora differt,
sentences.l: Pentheus looks at this man with eyes which anger had made terrible, and although he scarcely puts off the time of punishment,
sentences.i: Pentheus fixes him with eyes that rage had made terrible, and though he can barely bear to postpone the punishment,
sentences.n: 'quos ira tremendos fecerat' — 'which anger had made terrible': 'tremendus' is a gerundive used as an adjective, 'to be trembled at'. 'poenae vix tempora differt' = 'he barely puts off the moment of punishment'. The main verb ('ait', he says) is held back into the next unit, a suspension Ovid uses constantly — expect the sentence to finish two lines after it should.

sentences.t:
“o periture tuaque aliis documenta dature
morte” ait, “ede tuum nomen nomenque parentum
et patriam, morisque novi cur sacra frequentes.”
sentences.l: 'O you who are about to perish and to give a lesson to others by your death,' he says, 'declare your name and the name of your parents and your country, and why you attend the rites of the new custom.'
sentences.i: 'You who are about to die, and by your death to teach the rest a lesson,' he says, 'give me your name, your parents' names and your country — and why you keep the rites of this new fashion.'
sentences.n: Two future participles in the vocative, 'periture' and 'dature' — 'you who will perish', 'you who will give': Latin can address a man by what is about to happen to him, where English needs a whole clause. 'documenta' are object lessons, warnings made out of a person. 'moris novi' — 'of a new custom', Pentheus's contemptuous name for the worship of Bacchus; 'frequentes' is subjunctive in the indirect question after 'cur'.

sentences.t:
Ille metu vacuus “nomen mihi” dixit “Acoetes,
patria Maeonia est, humili de plebe parentes.
sentences.l: He, empty of fear, said 'my name is Acoetes, my country is Maeonia, my parents from the humble common people.
sentences.i: Free of fear, he said: 'My name is Acoetes, my country Maeonia, my parents common people of no rank.
sentences.n: 'metu vacuus' — 'empty of fear' (ablative of separation), the first thing said of him and the point of the whole speech that follows. 'nomen mihi ... Acoetes' is the dative of possession: 'to me the name is Acoetes'. Maeonia is Lydia in Asia Minor; at 696 the poem will call him Tyrrhenian (Etruscan) instead, and the ancients held the Etruscans to be emigrants out of Lydia, which is how both labels can stand.

sentences.t:
Non mihi quae duri colerent pater arva iuvenci,
lanigerosve greges, non ulla armenta reliquit;
sentences.l: My father left me no fields for tough bullocks to till, nor wool-bearing flocks, nor any herds at all;
sentences.i: My father left me no fields for stout oxen to work, no woolly flocks, no cattle at all;
sentences.n: Untangle the word order: 'pater' is the subject and 'reliquit' the verb, both pushed far from 'non mihi ... arva'. 'quae duri colerent ... iuvenci' is a relative clause of purpose with the subjunctive — 'fields which tough bullocks might till', i.e. fields for oxen to work. A catalogue of what a man did not inherit is how Ovid gives him a class.

sentences.t:
pauper et ipse fuit, linoque solebat et hamis
decipere et calamo salientes ducere pisces.
sentences.l: he too was poor himself, and with line and hooks he used to deceive, and with the rod to draw up, the leaping fish.
sentences.i: He was poor himself, and made his living deceiving fish with line and hook and drawing them up, still leaping, on the rod.
sentences.n: 'decipere' (deceive) is the ordinary Latin for taking fish on a baited hook — the fish is tricked, not caught. 'lino ... et hamis ... et calamo' are ablatives of means strung across the two lines, and 'salientes ... pisces' (the leaping fish) is the shared object of both infinitives, held to the very end.

sentences.t: Ars illi sua census erat. Cum traderet artem,
sentences.l: His skill was his fortune. When he was handing that skill on,
sentences.i: His craft was his whole estate. When he came to hand the craft on,
sentences.n: 'census' is a man's property as it stood in the censor's register — the Roman word for what you are worth, used here of a man who owned nothing but the knowledge of how to fish. 'illi' is again dative of possession ('to him his skill was his fortune'); 'cum traderet' is cum + imperfect subjunctive, 'when he was in the act of handing on'.

sentences.t:
“accipe quas habeo, studii successor et heres,”
dixit “opes.”
sentences.l: 'Receive what I have — you, successor and heir of my calling —' he said, 'my wealth.'
sentences.i: 'Take what riches I have,' he said, 'you who inherit and succeed to my calling.'
sentences.n: 'opes' (riches) is held back past the speech-tag 'dixit' so that it lands last: the wealth is the fishing. 'quas ... opes' is a relative clause wrapped around its own antecedent, normal in verse. 'studium' here is not study but a pursuit, the thing a man gives himself to.

sentences.t:
Moriensque mihi nil ille reliquit
praeter aquas: unum hoc possum appellare paternum.
sentences.l: And dying he left me nothing except the waters: this one thing I can call my father's.
sentences.i: And when he died he left me nothing but the water — that is the one inheritance I can call my father's.
sentences.n: 'moriens' (dying) is a present participle doing the work of an English clause. 'praeter aquas' — 'except the waters', the sea he fished. 'paternum' is a neuter adjective used as a noun, 'a thing of my father's', carrying the legal colour of an inheritance.

sentences.t:
Mox ego, ne scopulis haererem semper in isdem,
addidici regimen dextra moderante carinae
flectere
sentences.l: Soon I, so that I should not cling always to the same rocks, learned besides to bend the steering of the keel, my right hand guiding it,
sentences.i: Soon, so as not to be stuck on the same rocks for ever, I learned the further art of working a ship's helm, my right hand on the tiller,
sentences.n: 'ne ... haererem' is a negative purpose clause, 'so that I might not stick'. 'isdem' is Magnus's spelling of 'eisdem' (the same) and is kept as printed. 'dextra moderante' is an ablative absolute — a self-contained 'with my right hand guiding' where English wants a clause; you will meet this construction constantly in this poem. 'addidici' = 'I learned in addition' (ad- + disco).

sentences.t:
et Oleniae sidus pluviale capellae
Taygetenque hyadasque oculis arctonque notavi
ventorumque domos et portus puppibus aptos.
sentences.l: and with my eyes I marked the rainy star of the Olenian she-goat and Taygete and the Hyades and the Bear, and the houses of the winds and the harbours fit for ships.
sentences.i: and with my own eyes I marked the rainy star of the Olenian goat, Taygete and the Hyades and the Bear, the home of every wind, and the harbours a ship can use.
sentences.n: A navigator's whole syllabus, and almost all of it constellations. The 'Olenian goat' is Capella in Auriga, whose rising was held to bring rain; Taygete is one of the Pleiades and stands for the cluster; the Hyades are the rainy stars in the Bull; 'arcton' is a Greek accusative of 'arctos', the Great Bear, the group one steers by. 'ventorum domos' are the quarters of the sky each wind blows from.

sentences.t:
Forte petens Delum Chiae telluris ad oras
applicor et dextris adducor litora remis,
doque leves saltus udaeque inmittor harenae.
sentences.l: By chance, making for Delos, I put in at the shores of the land of Chios and am brought to the beach by well-handled oars, and I give light leaps and let myself down onto the wet sand.
sentences.i: Making for Delos as it happened, I put in on the coast of Chios, was rowed neatly to the beach, jumped lightly down and set myself on the wet sand.
sentences.n: 'applicor', 'adducor' and 'inmittor' are passive in form where English wants an active or reflexive sense — 'I bring myself in', 'I let myself down'; Latin often uses the passive for what a man does to himself. 'dexter' means both 'right-hand' and 'deft', and 'dextris ... remis' takes the second sense: oars well handled. 'litora' is a bare accusative of the goal of motion after 'adducor', ordinary in verse where prose would want a preposition. 'do saltus' — 'I give leaps' — is the standard idiom for jumping, and it will come back at 683 when the sailors leap for the last time.

sentences.t:
Nox ubi consumpta est (aurora rubescere prima
coeperat), exsurgo, laticesque inferre recentes
admoneo monstroque viam, quae ducat ad undas.
sentences.l: When the night had been used up — the first dawn had begun to redden — I get up, and urge them to bring on fresh water, and show the path which may lead to the springs.
sentences.i: When the night was spent — the early dawn had just begun to redden — I get up, tell the men to fetch fresh water, and show them the path down to the springs.
sentences.n: 'undas' here is fresh water, the spring, not the sea; 'latices ... recentes' fixes it. Watch the tenses: perfect and pluperfect set the scene, then 'exsurgo, admoneo, monstro' switch to the historic present and the story starts moving — a speed change Ovid works all through this speech. Magnus prints 'ubi' ('when') and 'prima'; some editions read 'ibi' ('there') and 'primo'.

sentences.t:
Ipse, quid aura mihi tumulo promittat ab alto
prospicio comitesque voco repetoque carinam.
sentences.l: I myself look out from a high mound to see what the breeze promises me, and I call my companions and make for the ship again.
sentences.i: From a high mound I look out for myself to see what the wind promises, then call the men and go back to the ship.
sentences.n: 'quid aura ... promittat' is an indirect question (subjunctive) governed by 'prospicio' — 'I look out to see what the breeze promises'. Sailors read the wind as a promise of the day's weather; the word is the trade's, not a metaphor invented for the passage. 'carina' (keel) stands for the whole ship, as 'pinus' and 'puppis' will.

sentences.t:
“Adsumus en!” inquit sociorum primus Opheltes,
utque putat, praedam deserto nactus in agro,
virginea puerum ducit per litora forma.
sentences.l: 'Here we are, see!' says Opheltes, first of the crew, and, having got — as he supposes — plunder in a deserted field, he leads along the shore a boy of maidenly beauty.
sentences.i: 'Here we are!' calls Opheltes, first of the crew, and he leads along the shore a boy of girlish beauty — booty, as he supposes, picked up in an empty field.
sentences.n: 'praeda' is plunder, and a captured human being counted as plunder: what Opheltes thinks he has is a boy to sell. 'ut putat' (as he supposes) is the older Acoetes marking the mistake before it is made. 'virginea ... forma' is an ablative of description, 'of maidenly beauty'; 'nactus' is the perfect participle of the deponent 'nanciscor', to come upon, to get.

sentences.t:
Ille mero somnoque gravis titubare videtur
vixque sequi.
sentences.l: He, heavy with unmixed wine and with sleep, seems to stagger and scarcely to follow.
sentences.i: The boy, heavy with neat wine and sleep, seems to stagger and barely to keep up.
sentences.n: 'merum' is wine drunk unmixed with water — for a Roman the mark of excess, and here of the god of wine himself, in disguise and overdoing it. 'gravis' governs the ablatives 'mero somnoque' (heavy with). 'videtur' + infinitive, 'seems to ...': Acoetes reports only how it looked.

sentences.t:
Specto cultum faciemque gradumque:
nil ibi quod credi posset mortale videbam.
sentences.l: I look at his dress and his face and his walk: I saw nothing there that could be believed mortal.
sentences.i: I study his clothes, his face, his walk: I could see nothing about him that anyone would take for mortal.
sentences.n: 'quod credi posset mortale' — 'which could be believed (to be) mortal': 'credi' is a passive infinitive with 'mortale' as its predicate, and 'posset' is subjunctive in a relative clause of characteristic ('nothing of the kind that could ...'). The three accusatives with -que ... -que pile the inspection up: dress, face, gait, in the order you would look at a stranger.

sentences.t:
Et sensi et dixi sociis: “Quod numen in isto
corpore sit, dubito; sed corpore numen in isto est.
sentences.l: And I perceived it and I said to my companions: 'What divinity is in that body, I doubt; but a divinity is in that body.
sentences.i: And I saw it, and I said so to the crew: 'Which god is in that body I cannot say; but a god is in that body.
sentences.n: The line turns the same four words twice: 'quod numen in isto corpore sit' (indirect question, subjunctive) and then 'corpore numen in isto est' (flat statement, indicative), re-ordered and with the mood changed. The doubt is only about which god, never about whether. 'iste' is the demonstrative of the person addressed — 'that one there, in front of you'.

sentences.t:
Quisquis es, o faveas nostrisque laboribus adsis.
His quoque des veniam.” —
sentences.l: Whoever you are, may you be favourable and stand by our labours. To these men also may you grant pardon.'
sentences.i: Whoever you are, be gracious to us and stand by our work — and pardon these men too.'
sentences.n: Three jussive subjunctives together — 'faveas, adsis, des' — the ordinary form of prayer, 'may you ...'. 'adsis' is the technical word for a god being present and on your side; 'quisquis es' is the standard formula for addressing a god whose name you do not know, so as not to name him wrongly. Acoetes asks pardon for the crew before they have done anything, which is the hinge of the whole tale. 'quoque' here is the plain adverb 'also'; the same letters elsewhere in this poem are 'quo-que', 'and with which', so check which one you have.

sentences.t:
“Pro nobis mitte precari”
Dictys ait, quo non alius conscendere summas
ocior antemnas prensoque rudente relabi.
sentences.l: 'Stop praying on our behalf,' says Dictys, than whom no other was quicker at climbing the topmost yardarms and, with the rope gripped, sliding back down.
sentences.i: 'Spare us your prayers,' says Dictys — and no man was quicker than he at going up to the topmost yards and sliding back down a rope.
sentences.n: 'mitte precari' — 'let go of praying', i.e. drop it: 'mitto' + infinitive is a brusque, colloquial dismissal. 'quo non alius ... ocior' is an ablative of comparison, 'than whom no other was swifter'. Ovid names his sailors and gives each one a skill, which is why their disappearance later costs the reader something. 'antemnas' is Magnus's spelling of the yardarm.

sentences.t:
Hoc Libys, hoc flavus, prorae tutela, Melanthus,
hoc probat Alcimedon, et qui requiemque modumque
voce dabat remis, animorum hortator Epopeus,
sentences.l: This Libys approves, this blond Melanthus, the guard of the prow, this Alcimedon approves, and he who with his voice gave rest and measure to the oars, the rouser of spirits, Epopeus,
sentences.i: Libys is of the same mind, and blond Melanthus the bow-watch, and Alcimedon, and Epopeus, who called the stroke and the rests to the oars and kept the men's hearts up —
sentences.n: One verb, 'probat' (approves), serves the whole roll-call, with 'hoc' (this) repeated four times as its object — a rhetorical hammering that makes the crew one voice. 'prorae tutela' is 'the prow's protection', the lookout at the bow, in apposition to Melanthus. Epopeus is the keleustes, the timekeeper who called the stroke and the pauses.

sentences.t: hoc omnes alii: praedae tam caeca cupido est.
sentences.l: this all the rest: so blind is the desire for plunder.
sentences.i: and all the rest the same: so blind is the lust for plunder.
sentences.n: The sentence ends on a sententia — the one-line judgement Acoetes steps back to deliver. 'praedae' is an objective genitive, 'desire for plunder', and 'caeca' (blind) is what that desire has done to men who have just been told there is a god aboard.

sentences.t:
“Non tamen hanc sacro violari pondere pinum
perpetiar” dixi: “pars hic mihi maxima iuris”;
sentences.l: 'Still, I will not endure this pine to be violated by a sacred burden,' I said: 'here the greatest part of the right is mine';
sentences.i: 'All the same, I will not have this ship profaned by a sacred cargo,' I said. 'The chief say here is mine.'
sentences.n: 'pinum' — pine, for the ship built of it: metonymy of the material, a standard move in verse. 'violari' is a passive infinitive in indirect statement after 'perpetiar' (I will endure), so literally 'I will not endure this pine to be violated'. 'sacro pondere' is ablative of means: the freight is sacred, and carrying it off is what does the violating. I take 'pars maxima iuris' as authority over the ship — Acoetes is the helmsman — rather than moral right; both readings are open.

sentences.t:
inque aditu obsisto. Furit audacissimus omni
de numero Lycabas, qui Tusca pulsus ab urbe
exsilium dira poenam pro caede luebat.
sentences.l: and in the gangway I plant myself. The boldest of the whole company rages, Lycabas, who, driven from an Etruscan city, was paying exile as a penalty for a dreadful killing.
sentences.i: and I plant myself in the gangway. Lycabas rages, the boldest of the whole crew — a man driven out of an Etruscan town, serving exile as his sentence for a savage murder.
sentences.n: 'aditus' is the way aboard, the gangway: Acoetes physically blocks it, having just claimed the authority to. 'exsilium ... poenam ... luebat' — 'was paying exile as a penalty': 'luo' is the verb for discharging a debt or a sentence, and the two accusatives sit side by side, the thing paid and what it counts as. Roman exile was the legal alternative to execution, so the line says Lycabas killed a man and kept his life. Magnus's spelling 'exsilium' is kept as printed.

sentences.t:
Is mihi, dum resto, iuvenali guttura pugno
rupit et excussum misisset in aequora, si non
haesissem, quamvis amens, in fune retentus.
sentences.l: He, while I stand firm, burst my throat with a youthful fist and would have sent me, knocked loose, into the sea, had I not stuck fast, senseless as I was, held back in a rope.
sentences.i: As I stood my ground he smashed my throat with a young man's fist, and would have knocked me overboard into the sea, had I not caught fast, dazed as I was, tangled and held in a rope.
sentences.n: A past contrary-to-fact condition: 'misisset ... si non haesissem' — 'he would have sent ... if I had not stuck', both pluperfect subjunctive. 'guttura' is a poetic plural for one throat. 'excussum' (shaken out, knocked loose) agrees with a 'me' that is never written. 'amens' is out of one's senses, here from the blow rather than from rage.

sentences.t:
Impia turba probat factum. Tum denique Bacchus
(Bacchus enim fuerat), veluti clamore solutus
sit sopor aque mero redeant in pectora sensus,
sentences.l: The godless crowd approves the deed. Then at last Bacchus — for Bacchus he had been all along — as though his sleep had been loosed by the shouting and his senses were coming back into his breast out of the wine,
sentences.i: The godless crew applauds. Then at last Bacchus — for Bacchus he was all along — acting as if the shouting had broken his sleep and his wits were coming back to him out of the wine,
sentences.n: 'impius' is the exact opposite of 'pius': not simply wicked, but in breach of what is owed to gods and men, and it is the word this whole tale is built on. 'veluti ... solutus sit ... redeant' is 'as if' + subjunctive — the reader is told plainly that the waking is a performance. 'Bacchus enim fuerat' is the storyteller stepping out of his own story to name what his younger self did not yet know.

sentences.t:
“quid facitis? quis clamor?” ait “qua, dicite, nautae,
huc ope perveni? quo me deferre paratis?”
sentences.l: 'What are you doing? what shouting is this?' he says. 'By what help, sailors, tell me, did I come here? where are you making ready to carry me?'
sentences.i: 'What are you doing? What is this shouting?' he says. 'Tell me, sailors — how did I get here? Where are you preparing to take me?'
sentences.n: 'qua ... ope' — 'by what help' — is wrapped around 'dicite, nautae' and completed only on the next line: the word order performs a man who cannot piece the night together. 'quo' is 'to where', not 'by which'. Four questions in two lines, and every one of them a lie.

sentences.t:
“Pone metum”, Proreus “et quos contingere portus
ede velis” dixit: “terra sistere petita.” —
sentences.l: 'Put down your fear,' said Proreus, 'and declare which harbours you wish to touch: you will be set down on the land you have asked for.'
sentences.i: 'Lay your fear aside,' said Proreus, 'and name the harbour you want to reach: you will be put ashore in the country you ask for.'
sentences.n: 'pone metum' — 'lay fear down', the ordinary idiom. 'quos contingere portus ... velis' is an indirect question with the subjunctive 'velis', its interrogative 'quos' pulled to the front of its clause. 'sistere' looks like an infinitive and is not: it is the alternative ending of the second-person singular passive (-re for -ris), so 'sisteris', 'you will be set down'. Verse uses this form freely and it catches every reader once. 'terra ... petita' is the ablative of place, the land asked for. Proreus's name is made from 'prora', the prow, like Melanthus's post at 617.

sentences.t:
“Naxon” ait Liber “cursus advertite vestros.
Illa mihi domus est, vobis erit hospita tellus.”
sentences.l: 'To Naxos,' says Liber, 'turn your courses. That is home to me; to you it will be a hospitable land.'
sentences.i: 'Naxos,' says Liber. 'Turn your course there. That island is my home; to you it will be a land of welcome.'
sentences.n: 'Naxon' is a Greek accusative (Greek -on where Latin would have -um), kept because the name is Greek — Ovid does this with Greek names throughout. 'Liber' is the old Italian god of wine identified with Bacchus, which lets the poem name him twice without repeating a word. 'mihi ... vobis' are datives of the person concerned, set against each other across the line, and the offered hospitality is exactly what the crew is about to break.

sentences.t:
Per mare fallaces perque omnia numina iurant
sic fore, meque iubent pictae dare vela carinae.
sentences.l: By the sea, the liars, and by all the divine powers they swear that it will be so, and they order me to give sails to the painted keel.
sentences.i: The liars swear by the sea and by every god that so it shall be, and they order me to make sail on the painted ship.
sentences.n: 'fallaces' (the deceivers) is dropped into the middle of the oath as the narrator's verdict on it — one adjective doing the work of a whole judgement. 'sic fore' is indirect statement, 'fore' being the future infinitive of 'sum': 'that it would be so'. 'dare vela' — 'to give sails (to the wind)' — is the standard idiom for setting sail. Swearing by 'omnia numina' while a numen stands on the deck is both the joke and the charge.

sentences.t:
Dextera Naxos erat. Dextra mihi lintea danti
“quid facis, o demens? quis te furor—?” inquit Opheltes.
sentences.l: Naxos was on the right. To me as I gave the sails to the right, 'What are you doing, madman? what madness has you—?' says Opheltes.
sentences.i: Naxos lay to starboard. As I set the sails to starboard, Opheltes bursts out: 'What are you doing, madman? What madness has hold of you—?'
sentences.n: 'Dextera ... Dextra' — the same word twice over, first 'Naxos was on the right', then 'to me giving the sails rightwards': the repetition is the argument, Acoetes doing precisely what the island required. 'mihi ... danti' is a dative participle, 'to me as I was giving'. The question breaks off unfinished at the dash; Ovid lets a sentence be interrupted. Magnus gives the line to Opheltes, but some editions read 'inquit Acoete', making it an unnamed voice that addresses Acoetes by name.

sentences.t:
Pro se quisque timet: “laevam pete” maxima nutu
pars mihi significat, pars quid velit aure susurrat.
sentences.l: Each fears for himself: 'make for the left', the greatest part signals to me with a nod, part whispers in my ear what it wants.
sentences.i: Each man is afraid for himself: 'bear left' — most of them signal it to me with a nod, others whisper in my ear what they want.
sentences.n: 'pro se quisque' — 'each on his own behalf', a set phrase: nobody on this ship is speaking for the ship. 'maxima ... pars' is split across the line-end and then picked up by a bare second 'pars' — 'the greater part ... another part'. 'quid velit' is an indirect question after 'susurrat'. Magnus prints 'timet' and 'aure susurrat'; some editions read 'tenet' and 'ore susurro'.

sentences.t:
Obstipui “capiat” que “aliquis moderamina” dixi
meque ministerio scelerisque artisque removi.
sentences.l: I was struck dumb, and 'let someone else take the steering,' I said, and I removed myself from the service both of the crime and of my craft.
sentences.i: I was struck dumb. 'Let someone else take the helm,' I said, and I took myself off from the work — the crime's and my craft's alike.
sentences.n: 'obstipui' is the perfect of a verb of stupor: struck motionless. 'capiat' is a jussive subjunctive, 'let him take'. The last line is the sharp one: 'ministerio sceleris ... artisque' — 'from the service of the crime and of my skill' — one noun governing both genitives, so that resigning his trade and refusing the crime become a single act.

sentences.t: Increpor a cunctis, totumque inmurmurat agmen.
sentences.l: I am shouted at by them all, and the whole company mutters.
sentences.i: They all round on me, and the whole company mutters.
sentences.n: 'increpor' is passive, 'I am rebuked, shouted at', with 'a cunctis' as the agent. 'inmurmurat' is Magnus's spelling of what other editions print 'immurmurat', kept as printed; the prefix carries the hostility — they mutter *at* him. 'agmen' is a body of men on the move, a word from the march, applied to a crew.

sentences.t:
E quibus Aethalion “te scilicet omnis in uno
nostra salus posita est” ait,
sentences.l: Out of whom Aethalion says 'in you alone, no doubt, all our safety is placed,'
sentences.i: One of them, Aethalion, says: 'So all our safety rests on you alone, does it,'
sentences.n: 'e quibus' is a connecting relative opening the sentence — 'and out of them' — where English simply starts a new sentence with 'one of them'; watch for this whenever a sentence begins with a form of 'qui'. 'scilicet' is the sarcasm marker, 'of course, naturally'. 'te ... in uno ... posita est' — the preposition splits the phrase — is the idiom for depending on someone: 'has been placed in you alone'.

sentences.t:
et subit ipse meumque
explet opus, Naxoque petit diversa relicta.
sentences.l: and he himself takes my place and fills out my task, and with Naxos left behind he makes for the opposite quarter.
sentences.i: and he steps into my place himself, takes over my job, and leaves Naxos behind to steer the other way.
sentences.n: 'subit' is 'goes in under', the word for relieving a man at his post. 'Naxo ... relicta' is another ablative absolute, 'with Naxos left behind'. 'diversa' is a neuter plural adjective used as a noun, 'the parts opposite' — Latin can turn an adjective into a place without help.

sentences.t:
Tum deus inludens, tamquam modo denique fraudem
senserit, e puppi pontum prospectat adunca
sentences.l: Then the god, mocking them, as though only now at last he had noticed the trick, looks out over the sea from the curved stern
sentences.i: Then the god, playing with them, as though only now had he seen through the trick, gazes out over the water from the curved stern
sentences.n: 'inludens' is playing upon them, the verb for mockery that keeps a straight face, and it governs the whole scene that follows. 'tamquam ... senserit' is 'as if' + subjunctive again — the second time in forty lines that the poem tells us the god is acting. 'e puppi ... adunca' tears the adjective away from its noun to the line's end, an ordinary poetic separation.

sentences.t:
et flenti similis “non haec mihi litora, nautae,
promisistis” ait, “non haec mihi terra rogata est.
sentences.l: and, like one weeping, he says 'these are not the shores, sailors, that you promised me; this is not the land I asked for.
sentences.i: and, like a boy in tears, he says: 'These are not the shores you promised me, sailors; this is not the land I asked for.
sentences.n: 'flenti similis' — 'like one weeping', with the dative that 'similis' takes; the point of 'similis' is that he is not weeping but looking as if. 'non haec ... non haec' repeats the denial at the head of each clause (anaphora). 'rogata est' is a passive of 'rogo' with the thing asked as its subject: 'the land was not asked for by me'.

sentences.t:
Quo merui poenam facto? quae gloria vestra est,
si puerum iuvenes, si multi fallitis unum?”
sentences.l: By what deed have I deserved punishment? what glory is yours, if you, grown men, cheat a boy, if many cheat one?'
sentences.i: What have I done to deserve punishment? What glory is there in it for you, if grown men cheat a boy, if a whole crew cheats one?'
sentences.n: 'quo ... facto' is an ablative of means split around the verb, 'by what deed'. The two 'si' clauses balance boy against men and one against many in the same shape — 'puerum iuvenes', 'multi ... unum' — with each pair jammed together so the mismatch is visible on the page. The god argues like a wronged child, which is precisely the performance.

sentences.t:
Iamdudum flebam: lacrimas manus impia nostras
ridet et impellit properantibus aequora remis.
sentences.l: For a long time now I had been weeping: the godless gang laughs at our tears and drives the sea on with hurrying oars.
sentences.i: I had been weeping for some time: the godless crew laughs at my tears and drives the water on with hurrying oars.
sentences.n: 'iamdudum' with the imperfect: Latin says 'I am weeping this long while' where English says 'I had been weeping'. 'manus' here is a band or gang of men, not a hand — the same word, and only the context decides; 'impia' again, the tale's key adjective. 'nostras' is a poetic plural for 'my'. Note that the oars drive the sea, not the ship: the water is what takes the blow.

sentences.t:
Per tibi nunc ipsum (nec enim praesentior illo
est deus) adiuro, tam me tibi vera referre,
quam veri maiora fide:
sentences.l: Now by the god himself I swear to you — for there is no god more present than he — that I report to you things as true as they are beyond the belief of truth:
sentences.i: Now I swear to you by the god himself — and no god is nearer at hand than he is — that what I am telling you is as true as it is past all believing:
sentences.n: 'per tibi ... adiuro' splits the preposition from its object with 'tibi' wedged in (tmesis) — 'by ... I swear to you ... the god himself'. 'praesentior' is the comparative of 'praesens' in its religious sense: a god who is *there*, at hand, effective. The last clause is compressed to paradox — 'as true as they are greater than truth's credit', true and unbelievable at once. And Acoetes is saying it to Pentheus, who is about to find out.

sentences.t:
stetit aequore puppis
haud aliter quam si siccum navale teneret.
sentences.l: the ship stood still on the open water no otherwise than if it were holding a dry dockyard.
sentences.i: the ship stood still on open water exactly as though it were sitting in a dry dock.
sentences.n: 'haud aliter quam si' + subjunctive introduces the comparison, 'no differently than if'. 'navale' is a ship-shed, the shed a hull is drawn up into out of the water, so the image is of a ship on land — motionless, which is the whole miracle. Magnus prints 'siccum', agreeing with 'navale'.

sentences.t:
Illi admirantes remorum in verbere perstant
velaque deducunt geminaque ope currere temptant.
sentences.l: They, marvelling, keep on at the beating of the oars and let the sails down and try to run with twofold help.
sentences.i: They wonder at it and keep beating away with the oars, let out the sails, and try to make her run under both together.
sentences.n: 'in verbere remorum' — 'at the lashing of the oars': rowing is a beating administered to the sea, and Ovid keeps the word. 'deducunt' of sails is letting canvas down from the yard, the opposite of furling. 'gemina ope' — 'by twin resource', oar and sail at once.

sentences.t:
Impediunt hederae remos nexuque recurvo
serpunt et gravidis distinguunt vela corymbis.
sentences.l: Ivies entangle the oars and with a curling knot creep, and pick the sails out with heavy clusters.
sentences.i: Ivy fouls the oars, creeps in curling coils, and picks the sails out with heavy clusters of berries.
sentences.n: The god's plant arrives with no verb of transformation and no warning — the ivy is simply there, doing the work of rigging. 'nexu recurvo' is an ablative of manner, 'with a bent-back twining'. 'corymbi' are the berry-clusters of ivy; 'distinguo' is the word for picking a surface out with ornament, as an embroiderer would, so the sails are being decorated and disabled in one motion.

sentences.t:
Ipse racemiferis frontem circumdatus uvis
pampineis agitat velatam frondibus hastam.
sentences.l: He himself, encircled as to his brow with cluster-bearing grapes, brandishes a spear veiled with vine-leaves.
sentences.i: The god himself, his brow wreathed in clustered grapes, shakes a spear veiled in vine leaves.
sentences.n: 'frontem circumdatus' is the Greek accusative of respect after a passive participle — 'encircled *as to* his forehead' — where English says 'with his brow wreathed'. Ovid uses this Greek construction constantly for dress and adornment; expect it again. The spear veiled in vine-leaves is the thyrsus, the wand carried by Bacchus and his followers: a weapon that does not look like one, and the weapon his mother throws at Pentheus at 712 to open the attack — the hands do the killing.

sentences.t:
Quem circa tigres simulacraque inania lyncum
pictarumque iacent fera corpora pantherarum.
sentences.l: Around whom lie tigers and empty likenesses of lynxes and the wild bodies of spotted panthers.
sentences.i: Around him lie tigers, phantom shapes of lynxes, and the wild bodies of spotted panthers.
sentences.n: 'quem circa' is a connecting relative with its preposition following it — 'and around him'; the reversal of preposition and noun is normal in verse. 'simulacra inania' — 'empty images': the beasts are apparitions, and Ovid says so of the lynxes only, leaving the tigers and panthers unqualified so that the reader cannot tell which are real. 'pictarum' of panthers means painted in the sense of spotted. The big cats are the god's beasts; Greek imagination brought his cult out of the East where they live.

sentences.t:
Exsiluere viri, sive hoc insania fecit,
sive timor, primusque Medon nigrescere coepit
corpore et expresso spinae curvamine flecti.
sentences.l: The men leapt out — whether madness did this or fear — and first Medon began to go black in body and to bend, the curve of his spine forced out.
sentences.i: The men leapt overboard, whether madness did it or fear; and Medon was the first to begin darkening in body and to bend, his spine forced up into a curve.
sentences.n: 'exsiluere' is the poetic third-person plural perfect in -ere for -erunt (= exsiluerunt): it is everywhere in verse and reads simply as 'they leapt'. 'expresso spinae curvamine' is an ablative absolute — 'with the curve of the spine pressed out' — which makes the change something done to him, not something he does. 'nigrescere' is an inceptive verb, 'to begin to be black': the -sc- suffix marks a change in progress, the exact shape a metamorphosis needs. Magnus reads 'coepit'; some editions print 'toto', giving 'to blacken over his whole body'.

sentences.t:
Incipit huic Lycabas: “In quae miracula” dixit
“verteris?”
sentences.l: Lycabas begins upon him: 'Into what marvels,' he said, 'are you being turned?'
sentences.i: Lycabas starts in on him: 'What sort of marvel are you being turned into?'
sentences.n: 'incipit huic' — 'begins at him', with a dative of the person addressed. 'in quae miracula verteris' is passive, 'into what wonders are you being turned': Latin has no need to say by whom, and the reader supplies the god. 'miraculum' is a thing to be wondered at, which in this poem means a thing that ought not to exist.

sentences.t:
et lati rictus et panda loquenti
naris erat, squamamque cutis durata trahebat.
sentences.l: and as he spoke there were wide gaping jaws and a bent-back nostril, and his hardened skin was drawing on a scaliness.
sentences.i: and even as he spoke his jaws gaped wide, his nostril curved back, and his hardening skin took on a coating of scales.
sentences.n: The verb 'erat' is singular with two subjects, ordinary enough in verse. 'loquenti' is a dative participle, 'to him as he was speaking' — the change overtakes the very sentence he is in the middle of, which is why the taunt has no ending. 'rictus' is properly the open gape of a beast's mouth; 'squamam trahebat' is the idiom for a body drawing on a covering.

sentences.t:
At Libys obstantes dum vult obvertere remos,
in spatium resilire manus breve vidit et illas
iam non esse manus, iam pinnas posse vocari.
sentences.l: But Libys, while he wants to turn the resisting oars, saw his hands spring back into a small compass, and that they were no longer hands, that they could now be called fins.
sentences.i: But Libys, trying to swing the blocked oars round, saw his hands shrink back into a little space — and that they were no longer hands, that they could now be called fins.
sentences.n: 'vidit' governs an indirect statement running to the end of the unit: 'manus resilire ... illas non esse ... posse vocari', three infinitives with 'manus / illas' as their accusative subject. 'in spatium ... breve' is split around 'resilire manus', 'into a small compass'. The finest touch is 'posse vocari', 'can be called': Ovid marks the moment the noun changes rather than the moment the thing does.

sentences.t:
Alter, ad intortos cupiens dare bracchia funes,
bracchia non habuit, truncoque repandus in undas
corpore desiluit:
sentences.l: Another, wanting to put his arms to the twisted ropes, had no arms, and bent backwards, his body docked, leapt down into the waves:
sentences.i: Another, meaning to set his arms to the twisted ropes, found he had no arms, and bent backwards, his body cut short, jumped down into the water:
sentences.n: 'bracchia ... bracchia' stands at the end of one line and the start of the next: the word is repeated at exactly the place where the arms are lost. 'trunco corpore' is an ablative of description, 'with a lopped body' — 'truncus' is the word for a trunk with the limbs cut off, and the poem will use it literally of Pentheus at 724. 'repandus' is bent backwards, the shape of a leaping dolphin.

sentences.t:
falcata novissima cauda est,
qualia dimidiae sinuantur cornua lunae.
sentences.l: his hindmost part is a sickle-curved tail, such as the horns of a half moon curve into.
sentences.i: his hindmost part is a sickle-shaped tail, curved like the horns of a half moon.
sentences.n: 'novissimus' is the Latin for 'last, hindmost' (literally 'newest'), so 'novissima cauda' is the tail at the very end of him. 'qualia' is neuter plural agreeing with 'cornua', the horns of the moon, to which the comparison is drawn. Some editions read 'dividuae' (divided) where Magnus prints 'dimidiae' (halved), with no change to the picture.

sentences.t:
Undique dant saltus multaque adspergine rorant
emerguntque iterum redeuntque sub aequora rursus
sentences.l: On all sides they give leaps and drip with much spray and emerge again and go back again beneath the water
sentences.i: They leap on every side and stream with spray, break the surface again and dive back under,
sentences.n: 'dant saltus' is the very idiom Acoetes used of himself jumping ashore at 599 — the men are still leaping, but now leaping is what they are. The four verbs strung on -que ... -que ... rursus imitate the rise and fall. 'adspergine' keeps Magnus's 'adsp-' spelling, which we do not normalise.

sentences.t:
inque chori ludunt speciem lascivaque iactant
corpora et acceptum patulis mare naribus efflant.
sentences.l: and they play into the appearance of a dance and toss their wanton bodies and blow out through wide nostrils the sea they have taken in.
sentences.i: and they play as though in a dance, tossing their bodies in sport, and blow out through wide nostrils the sea they have taken in.
sentences.n: 'in chori speciem' — 'into the likeness of a dance', the idiom for doing a thing in the shape of another thing. 'lascivus' is playful and unrestrained, with the sexual edge the word can carry left idle here. The last line is exact natural history — a dolphin's blowhole spray — and it is what convinces: the transformation ends in an animal that really behaves this way.

sentences.t:
De modo viginti (tot enim ratis illa ferebat)
restabam solus.
sentences.l: Out of twenty just now — for that many the ship was carrying — I alone was left.
sentences.i: Of the twenty there had been a moment before — that was the ship's whole complement — I alone was left.
sentences.n: 'de modo viginti' is compressed to the bone: 'out of the twenty of a moment ago', with the adverb 'modo' (just now) doing the work of a clause. The parenthesis is the only place in the tale the crew is counted. 'restabam' is imperfect — the state that went on, while the sea filled with dolphins.

sentences.t:
Pavidum gelidumque trementi
corpore vixque meum firmat deus “excute” dicens
“corde metum Diamque tene.”
sentences.l: The god steadies me — frightened and cold, with a trembling body, and scarcely my own — saying, 'shake the fear out of your heart, and hold for Dia.'
sentences.i: The god steadies me, terrified and cold, my body shaking, hardly myself, and says: 'Shake the fear out of your heart, and steer for Dia.'
sentences.n: Three accusatives all describing a 'me' that is never written: 'pavidum, gelidum, vix meum' — frightened, cold, and scarcely my own. 'vix meum' is the sharpest of them: he barely belongs to himself. 'excute corde metum' is a physical verb for a mental act, 'shake the fear out of your heart', and it is split across the speech-tag so the command lands in two pieces. Dia is another name for Naxos, so the god names the same island twice by two names.

sentences.t:
Delatus in illam
accessi sacris Baccheaque sacra frequento.”
sentences.l: Carried down to it, I joined the rites, and I keep the Bacchic rites.'
sentences.i: Brought there, I joined the god's worship, and I keep the rites of Bacchus to this day.'
sentences.n: 'accessi sacris' — 'I came to the rites', with the dative: the standard way of saying a man entered a cult. 'frequento' is present tense: he keeps them still, as he stands there under guard. And it is the same verb Pentheus threw at him in the first question of the interrogation ('cur sacra frequentes', 581), given back as the last word of the answer.

sentences.t:
“Praebuimus longis” Pentheus “ambagibus aures”
inquit “ut ira mora vires absumere posset.
sentences.l: 'We have lent our ears to long ramblings,' says Pentheus, 'so that anger might be able to spend its force in delay.'
sentences.i: 'We have given our ears to a long rambling tale,' says Pentheus, 'so that the delay might wear my anger out.'
sentences.n: Pure sarcasm, carried by the purpose clause: 'ut ... posset' states the intention Pentheus imputes to the story — it was told to run his rage down, and it has not. 'ambages' are windings, a roundabout way of speaking: the word for a tale that will not come to the point. 'praebuimus' is the royal plural: he answers as the crown, not as a man who has been listening.

sentences.t:
Praecipitem famuli rapite hunc cruciataque diris
corpora tormentis Stygiae demittite nocti.”
sentences.l: 'Servants, seize this man headlong, and send his body, tortured with dreadful torments, down to Stygian night.'
sentences.i: 'Seize the man and drag him off, slaves, and when his body has been broken with every dreadful torture, send it down into Stygian night.'
sentences.n: 'praecipitem ... hunc' — 'this man headlong': the adjective describes how he is to be taken, not what he is. 'corpora' is another poetic plural for one body. 'Stygiae ... nocti' is dative with 'demittite' — send him down to the dark of the Styx, i.e. kill him. The order names the torture first and the death second, which is the sequence Pentheus wants.

sentences.t:
Protinus abstractus solidis Tyrrhenus Acoetes
clauditur in tectis;
sentences.l: At once Tyrrhenian Acoetes, dragged off, is shut in a solid building;
sentences.i: At once Acoetes the Tyrrhenian is dragged away and shut in a strong-walled cell;
sentences.n: 'Tyrrhenus' is Etruscan, where Acoetes called himself a Maeonian at 583; the two labels stand together on the old belief about Lydia noted there. 'solidis ... in tectis' is 'within solid roofs', a poetic plural, with 'tectum' (roof) standing for the whole building.

sentences.t:
et dum crudelia iussae
instrumenta necis ferrumque ignesque parantur,
sponte sua patuisse fores lapsasque lacertis
sponte sua fama est nullo solvente catenas.
sentences.l: and while the cruel instruments of the ordered killing, iron and fires, are being prepared, the story is that of their own accord the doors stood open, and of their own accord the chains slipped from his arms, with no one loosing them.
sentences.i: and while the cruel instruments of the killing he had ordered — iron and fire — were being got ready, the story goes that the doors opened of themselves and the chains slipped of themselves from his arms, with nobody to unfasten them.
sentences.n: 'sponte sua' stands at the head of two successive lines, so the miracle is said twice before its subjects arrive. 'fama est' with the perfect infinitives 'patuisse ... lapsas (esse)' is indirect statement: the poem reports the escape as report and does not vouch for it, a deliberate half-step back from its own story. 'nullo solvente' is an ablative absolute whose subject is nobody at all. 'iussae ... necis' — the killing that had been ordered.

sentences.t:
Perstat Echionides. Nec iam iubet ire, sed ipse
vadit, ubi electus facienda ad sacra Cithaeron
cantibus et clara bacchantum voce sonabat.
sentences.l: The son of Echion persists. And now he does not order others to go, but himself goes, where Cithaeron, chosen for the rites that must be performed, was ringing with songs and the clear voice of the raving women.
sentences.i: The son of Echion holds to his course. Now he sends nobody: he goes himself, to where Cithaeron, chosen for the rites, rang with singing and the clear cries of the Bacchants.
sentences.n: 'Echionides' — 'son of Echion', a patronymic standing in for the name; Echion was one of the men who sprang from the sown dragon's teeth at the founding of Thebes, so the label quietly names whose city this is and how it was made. 'facienda ad sacra' is a gerundive, 'for the rites that are to be performed'. 'bacchantum' is the genitive plural participle of 'bacchor', to rave in the god's frenzy. Cithaeron is the mountain above Thebes — the same mountain on which Actaeon died earlier in this book, which Pentheus is about to be reminded of at 720.

sentences.t:
Ut fremit acer equus, cum bellicus aere canoro
signa dedit tubicen, pugnaeque adsumit amorem,
sentences.l: As a keen horse snorts when the war-trumpeter has given the signal on ringing bronze, and takes on a love of the fight,
sentences.i: As a spirited horse snorts when the trumpeter sounds the signal on ringing bronze, and takes on a passion for the battle,
sentences.n: The first half of a simile: 'ut ... sic' ('as ... so'), and the 'sic' does not arrive until the next unit. 'aere canoro' — 'with singing bronze', the trumpet named by its metal. 'adsumit amorem' is literally 'takes to itself a love (of the fight)': the horse catches the desire off the sound, which is exactly what the noise on the mountain is about to do to Pentheus. 'fremit' is the deep snorting rumble a horse makes in the chest, not a neigh.

sentences.t:
Penthea sic ictus longis ululatibus aether
movit, et audito clamore recanduit ira.
sentences.l: so the air, struck by long howls, stirred Pentheus, and at the shout heard his anger blazed white again.
sentences.i: so the air, struck with long howling, stirred Pentheus, and hearing the cry his anger flared white again.
sentences.n: 'Penthea' is the Greek accusative of the Greek name Pentheus, kept in its Greek form. The subject is 'aether', the air itself — struck like the trumpet's bronze in the simile and passing the blow on. 'audito clamore' is an ablative absolute, 'with the shout heard'. 'recanduit' is 'went white-hot again': 'candeo' is what metal does in a fire, and the 're-' says the anger had cooled while he listened to Acoetes.

sentences.t:
Monte fere medio est, cingentibus ultima silvis,
purus ab arboribus, spectabilis undique campus.
sentences.l: About halfway up the mountain there is, with woods ringing its edges, clear of trees, visible from every side, a plain.
sentences.i: About halfway up the mountain there is an open plain, ringed at its edges by woods, clear of trees and open to view from every side.
sentences.n: The noun 'campus' (plain) is held back to the very last word, after everything that describes it — a favourite arrangement in this poem, and worth expecting whenever a line starts with adjectives that agree with nothing yet. 'cingentibus ultima silvis' is an ablative absolute, 'with woods encircling its outermost parts'. The load-bearing phrase is 'spectabilis undique': the place is a natural theatre, and what happens in it is meant to be watched.

sentences.t:
Hic oculis illum cernentem sacra profanis
prima videt, prima est insano concita cursu,
prima suum misso violavit Penthea thyrso
mater.
sentences.l: Here she is first to see him watching the rites with profane eyes, first is she driven on in a mad run, first she wounded her own Pentheus with a hurled thyrsus — his mother.
sentences.i: Here his mother is the first to see him watching the rites with unhallowed eyes, the first to be driven into a mad rush, the first to wound her own Pentheus with a hurled thyrsus.
sentences.n: 'prima ... prima ... prima' opens three clauses in a row, and the subject of all three, 'mater', is withheld until the first word of the fourth line: the reader learns who it is at the worst possible moment, which is the whole design. 'oculis ... profanis' is an ablative of means — 'profanus' is the technical opposite of consecrated, a man not admitted to the rite. 'suum ... Penthea' — 'her own Pentheus'. The thyrsus is the vine-wrapped wand the god was shaking at 667, here thrown as a spear. 'violavit' is the verb Acoetes used at 621 of the ship being desecrated, now used of a son.

sentences.t:
“Io, geminae” clamavit “adeste sorores!
ille aper, in nostris errat qui maximus agris,
ille mihi feriendus aper.”
sentences.l: 'Io! twin sisters,' she cried, 'be here! that boar, the huge one that wanders in our fields — that boar is mine to strike.'
sentences.i: 'Io! Sisters, both of you,' she cried, 'come to me! That boar, the huge one that roams our fields — that boar is mine to strike down.'
sentences.n: 'io' is the ritual cry of the god's worshippers, a sound rather than a word, and it is left as it stands; some editions read 'et o' here. 'geminae ... sorores' are Autonoë and Ino, her two sisters. 'ille aper ... ille ... aper' frames the sentence with the same two words: this is not a figure of speech — in her madness she sees a boar. 'mihi feriendus' is a gerundive with the dative of the agent, 'to be struck by me', the ordinary Latin for 'mine to strike'.

sentences.t:
Ruit omnis in unum
turba furens; cunctae coeunt trepidumque sequuntur,
sentences.l: The whole raving crowd rushes upon the one man; all the women come together and pursue him as he trembles,
sentences.i: The whole raving crowd rushes at the one man; they gather from every side and chase him as he shakes,
sentences.n: 'omnis ... turba' against 'in unum' — the crowd and the one man set at opposite ends of the line. 'coeunt' is 'go together', the same verb used of an assembly forming, so the hunt has the shape of a gathering. 'trepidum' (trembling, in a panic) is an adjective standing in for him, and the next line will take it up and repeat it. 'cunctae' is feminine, so the poem never has to say what the crowd is made of: the adjective has already said it.

sentences.t:
iam trepidum, iam verba minus violenta loquentem,
iam se damnantem, iam se peccasse fatentem.
sentences.l: now trembling, now speaking less violent words, now condemning himself, now confessing that he had done wrong.
sentences.i: trembling now; speaking less violently now; condemning himself now; now admitting that he had done wrong.
sentences.n: Four clauses, each opening with 'iam' (now), each a step further down: fear, then softer words, then self-condemnation, then confession. 'se peccasse fatentem' is an indirect statement inside a participle — 'confessing himself to have sinned' — with 'peccasse' the syncopated form of 'peccavisse'. Ovid gives Pentheus his change of mind exactly one line too late for it to matter.

sentences.t:
Saucius ille tamen “fer opem, matertera” dixit
“Autonoë! moveant animos Actaeonis umbrae.”
sentences.l: Wounded, he still said, 'bring help, mother's sister Autonoë! let the shade of Actaeon move your heart.'
sentences.i: Wounded, he still says: 'Help me, Aunt Autonoë! Let Actaeon's ghost move your heart.'
sentences.n: 'matertera' is precisely a mother's sister — Latin keeps a separate word for the father's — and the exactness of the kinship is the whole force of the appeal. Actaeon was Autonoë's own son, torn apart by his own hounds on this same mountain: Pentheus is asking her to remember a death like the one now being done to him. 'moveant ... umbrae' is a jussive subjunctive with a poetic plural for one ghost.

sentences.t:
Illa, quis Actaeon, nescit dextramque precantis
abstulit: Inoo lacerata est altera raptu.
sentences.l: She does not know who Actaeon is, and she carried off the right hand of the man praying: the other was mangled by an Inoan snatching.
sentences.i: She does not know who Actaeon is, and she tore off the suppliant's right hand; the other was mangled by Ino's snatching.
sentences.n: 'quis Actaeon' is an indirect question with its verb left out — 'who Actaeon is' — and 'nescit' follows it: the madness has taken even the name of her own son. 'abstulit' is the plain verb 'carried off', doing terrible work by understatement, and 'precantis' is the participle as a noun, 'of the man praying'. 'Inoo ... raptu' is 'by an Inoan snatching', an adjective coined from Ino's name where English needs a possessive; the passive 'lacerata est' leaves the arm as the subject and the sister half out of the sentence.

sentences.t:
Non habet infelix quae matri bracchia tendat,
trunca sed ostendens deiectis vulnera membris
“adspice, mater!” ait.
sentences.l: The unhappy man has no arms to stretch out to his mother, but showing his lopped wounds, his limbs cast off, he says, 'look, mother!'
sentences.i: The wretched man has no arms left to stretch out to his mother, but he shows the maimed wounds, his limbs torn from him, and says: 'Look at me, mother!'
sentences.n: 'quae ... tendat' is a relative clause of purpose with the subjunctive: 'arms of the kind he might stretch out', i.e. no arms to reach with. The sentence is built so that the loss registers as the failure of a gesture — the one movement a child makes towards a parent. 'trunca ... vulnera' are 'lopped wounds', the wound named for the cut that made it, and 'truncus' is the word used of the sailor's docked body at 680. Magnus prints 'deiectis' (cast down); some editions read 'dereptis' (torn away). 'deiectis membris' is an ablative absolute, 'with the limbs thrown down'.

sentences.t:
Visis ululavit Agaue
collaque iactavit movitque per aera crinem
sentences.l: At these things seen Agave howled, and tossed her neck and shook her hair through the air
sentences.i: At the sight Agave howled, threw back her head and shook her hair on the air,
sentences.n: 'visis' is an ablative absolute made of nothing but a participle — 'these things having been seen' — and it is the whole of her answer to what she has just been shown. 'colla' is another poetic plural for one neck. The thrown-back head and streaming hair are the fixed posture of a woman in the god's possession, so Ovid replies to a son's appeal with a description of the dance.

sentences.t:
avulsumque caput digitis complexa cruentis
clamat “io comites, opus haec victoria nostrum est!”
sentences.l: and having clasped the torn-off head in her bloody fingers she cries, 'Io, comrades! this victory is our work!'
sentences.i: and clutching the torn-off head in her bloody fingers she cries: 'Io, companions! This victory is our doing!'
sentences.n: 'complexa' is the perfect participle of the deponent 'complector' and is active in sense, 'having embraced' — and embrace is the word, used of a mother holding her son's head. 'io' is the cult cry again, the same sound she called her sisters with at 713. 'opus ... nostrum' is 'our work' in the sense of a made thing, a craftsman's product. Magnus reads 'opus haec victoria nostrum est' ('this victory is our work'); some editions print 'hoc ... nostra', which reverses it to 'this work is our victory'.

sentences.t:
Non citius frondes autumni frigore tactas
iamque male haerentes alta rapit arbore ventus,
quam sunt membra viri manibus direpta nefandis.
sentences.l: Not more swiftly does the wind snatch from a high tree the leaves touched by autumn's cold and already barely holding, than the man's limbs were torn apart by those unspeakable hands.
sentences.i: No faster does the wind strip from a high tree the leaves that autumn's cold has touched and that already hardly hold, than the man's limbs were torn from him by those unspeakable hands.
sentences.n: 'non citius ... quam' — 'not more quickly than' — frames the whole comparison, and the proportions are the point: two lines for the leaves, half of one for the body. 'tactas' and 'haerentes' both belong to the leaves, touched by frost and already loosening. 'nefandus' is literally 'not to be spoken of', the strongest word Latin has for an act outside what may be said aloud — and the hands are his mother's and his aunts'.

sentences.t:
Talibus exemplis monitae nova sacra frequentant
turaque dant sanctasque colunt Ismenides aras.
sentences.l: Warned by such examples, the women of Ismenus attend the new rites, and give incense and worship the holy altars.
sentences.i: Warned by such examples, the women of Thebes keep the new rites, offer incense and tend the sacred altars.
sentences.n: 'talibus exemplis monitae' is a participle agreeing with the subject and doing the work of an ablative absolute, 'having been warned by such examples' — and 'exempla' answers the 'documenta' Pentheus promised at 579, when he told Acoetes his death would be a lesson to others. The lesson was made out of Pentheus instead. 'Ismenides' are the Theban women, named from the river Ismenus. The tale closes on 'frequentant', the verb Pentheus used in contempt at 581 and Acoetes used in devotion at 691.
